points: A data structure provides the *how*: the concrete implementation that fulfills the interface’s specification.
The interface can be viewed as a specification of desired behavior, while the data structure is the actual storage mechanism.
The interface specifies which operations are supported and what they mean, while the data structure provides concrete algorithms to implement those operations.
Algorithms are the methods a data structure uses to support the operations defined by the interface.
The course will concentrate on two primary interfaces and their special cases, emphasizing the separation of what to do from how to do it.
A problem statement can have many algorithmic solutions; similarly, a data‑structure problem can be solved by different structures that implement the same operations.
Different data structures may support the same operations but with different performance characteristics, so the choice depends on which operations are critical for your use case.
We will focus on two fundamental abstract data types: the set and the sequence, each with its own typical operations and use‑cases.
If we need the elements kept in sorted order and searchable by a value (the *key*), the data structure must support ordering and efficient lookup.
Python list can store elements and preserves insertion order.
The list will maintain the order: first, second, last items.
We will focus on the sequence data structure for now, with set interface mentioned later.
The lecture notes mention that structures will bounce back and forth between these concepts, which are closely related and abstract.
Intro to Algorithms is taught by Jason Ku together with faculty Eric Domen and Justin Solomon.
The course emphasizes not just solving problems but also proving that your solution is correct and efficient.
The class will involve a lot of writing to convey algorithmic ideas clearly to others.
A computational problem is a binary relation between a set of inputs and a set of outputs.
For each input, the problem specifies which outputs are correct; there may be more than one correct output.
The lecturer illustrates a computational problem as a mapping from inputs to outputs, where an input may map to multiple outputs.
The mapping can be visualized as a graph, with edges representing the binary relation between inputs and outputs.
This is the first class of 6.001 and 6.600 this semester, taught by Anna Bell with later lectures by Prof. Eric Grimson.
The lecture will later cover basic administrative info and a high‑level discussion of what computation is—i.e., what computers do.
We'll dive into Python basics, starting with mathematical operations and then Python types.
All lecture slides and code examples will be uploaded before class; students are encouraged to download them in advance.
Class exercises are embedded in the slides; taking notes on the code is recommended for future reference.
The course moves quickly, so students should adopt strategies early to succeed.
Practice is essential for new programmers; regular coding improves skill just like math or reading.
Practice is essential; you must type code and experiment regularly.
Don’t fear breaking your computer—just restart it after trying commands in Anaconda.
The course focuses on three outcomes: conceptual knowledge, programming skills, and problem‑solving ability.
The course content is divided into three main sections.
The first section focuses on learning how to program, including choosing objects to create.
